title: Feelings: naming them, and what helps when we feel sad or angry

summary.text: Stop for a moment and ask yourself: what am I feeling right now? Happy, sad, angry, scared and calm are all feelings, and every person has every one of them. Your child names their feelings, and draws a face for each one, six times in one day. They find out whether one feeling stays all day or many feelings come and go. They also try things that help when a feeling is sad or angry: a slow breath, a hug, a quiet watch, and saying the feeling out loud.
summary.art: A sheet of paper with six circles on it, each with a different child-drawn face: happy, cross, calm, sleepy, sad and happy again, with crayons beside it on a floor mat.

intro.hook: Put your hand on your tummy and close your eyes. What are you feeling right now? Can you give it a name?
intro.text: A feeling is something you notice inside you. Happy is a feeling. So are sad, angry, scared and calm. Every person has all of these, and so do many other animals. In this unit you give your feelings names. You draw your feelings through one whole day. And you find out what helps when a feeling is sad or angry.
intro.art: A child sitting cross-legged on a mat with eyes closed and one hand on their tummy, with a small question mark above their head.

outcomes: By the end I can name at least five feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared and calm.
By the end I can say what I am feeling, and how big the feeling is.
By the end I can say that every feeling is all right to have, even anger and sadness.
By the end I can show that my feelings change many times in one day.
By the end I can name things that help when I feel sad or angry, like a slow breath, a hug or telling someone.
By the end I can say that hitting or shouting does not make anger go away.

terms.meaning: A feeling is something you notice inside you, in your body and in your thoughts. Happy, sad, angry and scared are feelings.
terms.example: When your friend shares her mango with you, you feel happy.
terms.art: A child smiling as a friend hands her half a ripe mango.

terms.meaning: Emotion is the word scientists use for a feeling like happy, sad, angry or scared.
terms.example: Fear is an emotion. Your heart beats fast when a loud firecracker bursts nearby.
terms.art: A child jumping in surprise at a firecracker going off in the street during Diwali, with a heart drawn beating fast.

terms.meaning: Calm is a quiet, steady feeling. Your body is still, and your breath is slow.
terms.example: Lying on the bed after a bath, listening to the rain, you may feel calm.
terms.art: A child lying on a bed with eyes half closed, rain falling outside a window.

terms.meaning: To comfort someone is to help them feel better when they are sad, hurt or scared.
terms.example: When a younger child falls and cries, you can comfort him with a hug.
terms.art: A girl kneeling and hugging a younger child who has fallen and scraped a knee.

terms.meaning: Well-being means your body and your feelings are both looked after.
terms.example: Sleep, food, water, play and people who listen to you are all part of your well-being.
terms.art: A small circle of pictures: a bed, a plate of food, a tumbler of water, a ball, and two people talking.

explanations.definition: A feeling, or emotion, is something that happens inside you when something happens to you or around you. You notice it in your body and in your thoughts.
explanations.description: Feelings happen in your whole body. A scared heart beats fast. An angry face gets hot, and a sad throat gets tight. Giving the feeling a name is the first step to knowing it.
examples: A dog barks suddenly, and your heart thumps. That is fear.
Your tower of blocks falls down, and your face gets hot. That is anger.
A cousin you love goes back home after a visit, and you feel tears coming. That is sadness.
explanations.context: This card says what a feeling is.
explanations.art: Four small pictures of the same child: heart thumping beside a barking dog, red face beside a fallen tower of blocks, a tear while waving goodbye at a door, and a big laugh.

explanations.concept: Every feeling is all right to have
explanations.definition: Every feeling is a normal part of being a person. No feeling is a bad feeling, though some feel hard.
explanations.description: Everyone feels angry sometimes, and everyone feels sad: grown-ups, children, girls and boys. Fear helps you keep away from danger. Sadness tells the people around you that you need comfort. What we do with a feeling matters, so hitting hurts someone, but the feeling itself is all right.
examples: Fear makes you step back from a busy road.
When you cry, a grown-up near you knows you need a hug.
Anger tells you something is unfair, like your turn on the swing being taken.
explanations.context: This card says that no feeling is a bad feeling.
explanations.art: A child stepping back from the edge of a busy road with cars and autos going past, holding a grown-up's hand.

explanations.definition: Feelings change. A feeling comes, it may get bigger, then it gets smaller and goes. A new feeling comes in its place.
explanations.description: In one day you may feel sleepy, then happy, then cross, then calm, then excited. Some feelings pass in a few minutes, and sadness often stays longer. Scientists have found that a feeling lasts longer when we keep thinking about what caused it. Playing or helping often lets it change sooner.
examples: You feel cross when it is time to stop playing. Ten minutes later you are laughing at dinner.
You feel scared at the start of a thunderstorm. After a while, you feel calm and watch the rain.
You feel sad when a friend moves away. The sadness comes back sometimes, but it gets smaller over the weeks.
explanations.context: This card is about how feelings change through a day.
explanations.art: A row of five faces drawn by a child, labelled with clock times from morning to night: sleepy, happy, cross, calm, excited.

explanations.description: Saying a feeling's name out loud often helps: 'I am angry.' 'I feel sad.' In 2007, Matthew Lieberman, Naomi Eisenberger and their team in the USA showed people angry and scared faces. When people picked a word for the feeling, a part of the brain that reacts to fear got quieter. Lisa Feldman Barrett and her team found that people who know many feeling words often handle hard feelings better. Naming does not always make a feeling go away, but it often makes it a little smaller, and scientists are still finding out why.
examples: Saying 'I am cross because my drawing got torn' often helps more than shouting.
A small child who says 'I'm scared of the dark' can be helped to switch on a night light.
Knowing the word 'disappointed' helps you say exactly how you feel when a trip is cancelled.
explanations.context: This card is about why saying the name of a feeling helps.
explanations.art: A child with fists clenched saying 'I am angry!' to her mother, with a small cloud above her head getting smaller.

explanations.concept: What helps when you feel sad or angry
explanations.description: Many things help when a feeling is big: slow breaths, telling someone, a hug, a quiet place, a drink of water or a rest. Crying is all right too. Many people used to think the best thing for anger was to let it out by hitting a pillow or shouting. Scientists tested this, and found it usually makes anger last longer. Slow breathing works better.
examples: Five slow breaths, in through the nose and out through the mouth.
Telling a grown-up, 'I am sad because my balloon burst.'
Sitting in a quiet corner with a soft toy until the feeling gets smaller.

perspectives.explanation: Anger builds up inside you. If you don't let it out by shouting or hitting a pillow, it will burst out later.

perspectives.who: Brad Bushman, Sophie Kjærvik and other scientists who tested it
perspectives.explanation: Hitting things while angry usually keeps anger going. Calming things like slow breathing, relaxing and taking time out make anger smaller.
A feeling should not be pushed down and hidden either. Saying it in words, to someone who listens, is the healthy way to let it out.

explanations.context: This card is about the things that help with big, hard feelings.
explanations.art: A child sitting on a floor cushion, breathing out slowly with puffed cheeks, while an older person sits beside them with an arm round their shoulders.

explanations.description: Humans are animals, and many other animals have feelings too. A dog wags her tail and jumps when someone she loves comes home. Young rats make tiny squeaking calls when they are tickled, too high for us to hear. Jaak Panksepp, a scientist in the USA, called it rat laughter. After a fight, one chimpanzee often hugs another who was hurt. A touch-me-not plant folds up her leaves when touched, but scientists do not agree that this is a feeling. Scientists argue about how much other beings feel, and whether their feelings are like ours.
examples: A cat purrs and rubs against your leg when she is content.
A crow caws loudly and swoops when someone goes near her nest.
A touch-me-not plant folds up her leaves when a finger touches them. Is that a feeling? Scientists are not sure.

perspectives.explanation: Dogs, rats, crows, chimpanzees and many other animals feel joy, fear and anger. We can see it in what they do, and their bodies change as ours do.
We can watch what other beings do, but we cannot be inside them. So we should not be sure their feelings are like ours. A plant folding her leaves may be a feeling very different from our fear.

explanations.context: This card is about feelings in humans and other animals.
explanations.art: A happy dog jumping up at a girl coming in through a flat's front door, with a touch-me-not plant in a pot on the windowsill, leaves folded.

agreed.text: Every person has feelings like happy, sad, angry and scared. All of them are normal.
agreed.evidence: Scientists and doctors who have studied children and grown-ups in many countries find these feelings in everyone.

agreed.text: Feelings happen in the body as well as the mind.
agreed.evidence: When people feel scared or angry, doctors can measure their heart beating faster and their breathing changing.

agreed.text: Hitting or shouting does not make anger go away. Calming the body helps more.
agreed.evidence: In 2024, Sophie Kjærvik and Brad Bushman put together more than 150 studies. Calming activities like slow breathing lowered anger. Venting did not help, and sometimes made anger bigger.

agreed.text: Children cope better with hard feelings when they have someone to talk to.
agreed.evidence: Studies that follow children as they grow find that children with a caring grown-up to talk to recover from hard times better.

challenging.who: An old saying, heard in many families
challenging.for: Some people think crying shows that a boy is not strong.
challenging.against: Boys and girls have the same feelings, and both need comfort. Crying is one way the body shows sadness and asks for help. Hiding feelings does not make them go away.
challenging.context: This card is about an old saying about boys and crying.

challenging.claim: When you are angry, hit a pillow to let the anger out.
challenging.who: A popular idea, still given as advice by some people
challenging.for: Hitting a pillow hurts no one, and some people say they feel better for a moment.
challenging.against: Scientists tested this many times. People who hit things while angry stayed angrier than people who sat quietly. Slow breathing and calming down worked better.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular idea for anger.

challenging.who: Something many children believe, and some grown-ups say
challenging.for: Grown-ups enjoy seeing children happy, and children want to please them.
challenging.against: Every child feels sad, angry and scared sometimes. These feelings are normal and do useful jobs. A child who can say 'I feel sad' is doing well, not badly.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that children should always be happy.

big_questions.q: Your feelings changed many times today. Were you the same you all day long?
big_questions.hint: Think of the happy you at breakfast and the cross you later on. Who was there both times?

big_questions.q: Where is a feeling? Is it in your tummy, your heart, your head, or everywhere?
big_questions.hint: Put your hand where you feel it the next time you are scared or happy.

big_questions.q: Can a crow, a cat or a plant feel sad? How could we find out?
big_questions.hint: Think about what they do when something bad happens to them.

big_questions.q: Why does saying 'I am angry' make anger feel a little smaller?
big_questions.hint: Scientists are still finding out. What do you think happens inside you?

story.title: Chinnu's Sandcastle
story.note: Chinnu, her Chitti and the boy are made up. Marina Beach in Chennai is real. Naming a feeling and slow breathing really do help many children calm down.
text: Chinnu was six. She lived in a flat in Chennai, near the sea, with her mother and her Chitti. Chitti was her mother's younger sister. On Sunday evenings, Chitti took Chinnu to Marina Beach.

This Sunday, Chinnu had a plan. She wanted to build the biggest sandcastle on the whole beach. She brought a steel tumbler, a small bucket and a spoon. Chitti carried water from the sea in the bucket. Chinnu packed wet sand into the tumbler and turned it over. Pat, pat, lift. A tower! Then another, and another. Soon there were five towers, with a wall all round them. Chinnu stuck a shell on the top of each tower.
'It is the best castle I have ever made,' she said. She felt so happy that she did a little dance.

Just then, a big red ball came bouncing across the sand. A boy came running after it. He did not look where he was going. His foot went right into the castle. Two towers fell flat. The wall broke. A shell rolled away.
'Sorry!' the boy shouted, and he ran off with his ball.

Chinnu's face went hot. Her hands made fists. She stamped her foot so hard that sand flew up. 'He broke it! He broke my castle!' she shouted. She wanted to kick the rest of the castle down. She wanted to throw sand at the boy.
Chitti knelt down next to her. She did not say 'Stop that'. She did not say 'It is only sand'. She said, 'What are you feeling, Chinnu?'
'I don't know!' Chinnu shouted. Then she stopped. Her face was hot. Her hands were tight. 'Angry,' she said. 'I am angry.'
'Yes,' said Chitti. 'You worked hard, and he broke it. Anyone would feel angry. Is there another feeling too?'
Chinnu looked at the flat towers. Her throat felt tight. Tears came. 'Sad,' she said, very quietly. 'I am sad too.'

Chitti held out her arms, and Chinnu climbed into them. 'Let's do the wave breath,' said Chitti. 'Breathe in slowly while the wave comes in. Breathe out slowly while the wave goes back.' They watched the sea. A wave came in, and they breathed in. The wave went back, and they breathed out. They did it five times.
Chinnu's hands were not tight any more. Her face was not so hot. The angry feeling was still there, but it was smaller now. The sad feeling was smaller too.
'Chitti,' said Chinnu, 'my angry feeling got little.'
'Feelings do that,' said Chitti. 'They come, they get big, and then they change. You gave them names. You breathed, and you let me hug you. That helped them change.'
Just then the boy came back. He was holding a big white shell. 'I'm really sorry I broke your castle,' he said. 'This is for you. Can I help you build it again?'
Chinnu thought about it. A small bit of anger was still there. But mostly she felt something else now. 'Yes,' she said. 'You bring the water.'
They built the castle again, with six towers this time. The big white shell went on the tallest one. When the sun went down, Chinnu was tired and sandy, and happy.
On the bus home, she counted on her fingers. 'Happy, angry, sad, calm, happy,' she said. 'That is a lot of feelings for one beach.'
story.epiphany: Chinnu names her two feelings, angry and sad. After slow breaths and a hug, she notices that the angry feeling has got smaller. She sees that feelings change, and that naming them and calming her body helped.
ask: What two feelings did Chinnu have when her castle broke?
What did Chitti do that helped? What did she not say?
On the bus, Chinnu counted her feelings: happy, angry, sad, calm, happy. Which feeling came two times? What feelings did you have today?
art: A girl of six on a sunny beach in Chennai, turning a steel tumbler over to make a sand tower, with five towers topped by shells.
A girl stamping her foot with fists clenched beside a broken sandcastle, while a boy runs off with a red ball.
A young woman kneeling on the sand and hugging the girl, both watching a wave come in.

how_we_found_out.context: Does hitting a pillow let your anger out? This card tells how scientists found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people believed that anger builds up inside you. If you do not let it out, they said, it will burst out later. So people were told to hit a pillow or a punching bag when angry. Brad Bushman, a scientist in the USA, tested this in a study published in 2002. He made about 600 students cross with a rude note about their writing. One group hit a punching bag while thinking about the rude person. A second group hit the bag while thinking about getting fit. A third group sat quietly. The students who hit the bag thinking about the rude person were the angriest, and the meanest to that person. The students who sat quietly were the least angry. In 2024, Sophie Kjærvik and Brad Bushman put together more than 150 studies. Calming things, like slow breathing, made anger smaller. So the old idea was wrong.
how_we_found_out.who: Brad Bushman, an American scientist who studies anger, and Sophie Kjærvik, who led the 2024 review of more than 150 studies with him
how_we_found_out.when: Bushman's punching bag study was published in 2002. The review of more than 150 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman was published in 2024.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That anger builds up inside like steam, so hitting a pillow or shouting lets it out and makes you calm. The tests showed that hitting things while angry keeps the anger going, and calming the body makes it smaller.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist at a table with piles of papers and a chart with two bars, one tall and red, one short and blue, and a small drawing of a person breathing slowly.

experiments.title: My Feelings Chart: how many feelings come in one day?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stop six times in one day and ask yourself what you are feeling. You draw a face for each feeling. Then you look at the whole day.
experiments.question: In one day, do I have one feeling all day, or many different feelings? When a sad or cross feeling comes, does it stay?
experiments.predict: How many different feelings do you think you will draw today? Will one feeling stay all day? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We stop at the same six times in the day: waking up, breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, late afternoon and bedtime. Each time, you name the feeling yourself. Nobody tells you what you feel. Any feeling is a right answer.
results_table: How big? small, middle or big
If it was sad, cross or scared: what helped?

materials.item: a sheet of paper with six big circles drawn on it, in two rows of three
a clock or a phone to see the time
sticky tape, to put the chart on the wall or the fridge

schedule.what: Make the chart, guess how many feelings will come, and draw the first face when you wake up or soon after.
Stop five more times in the day, at breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, late afternoon and bedtime, and draw a face each time. If a face is sad, cross or scared, try one helper.
Look at the whole chart. Count the different feelings. Did any feeling stay all day? Compare with your guess.

experiments.record: The chart of six faces, with a small picture next to any sad, cross or scared face showing what helped.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: Lakshmi's chart, age 6
rows: Five slow breaths, and a grown-up sharpened it
A hug and a new story

setup.art: A child drawing six big circles on a sheet of paper on the floor, with crayons around, and a parent writing small times under the circles: wake up, breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, afternoon, bedtime.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six circles. A grown-up writes the six times.

setup.art: A child standing still in a kitchen with one hand on their tummy and eyes closed, thinking.
setup.caption: 2. Stop. Hand on your tummy. What am I feeling?

setup.art: A child drawing a cross face with eyebrows down in the third circle of the chart taped to a fridge door.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the face in the right circle.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up looking at the finished chart of six different faces, counting on their fingers.
setup.caption: 4. Next day: count the different feelings.

flow.do: 1. Draw six big circles on the paper. 2. Under them, write the six times: wake up, breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, afternoon, bedtime. 3. Tape the chart where your child can reach it.
flow.say: Today we are going to be feeling scientists. Six times today, we will stop and ask what you are feeling. You will draw a face for it in a circle.
flow.kid: Today you are a feeling scientist. Six times today, you stop. You ask: what am I feeling? You draw the face.
flow.parent: The fridge door or a wall at child height works well. Write the times small, under the circles. Your child does the drawing.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess. Write their guess at the top of the chart.
flow.say: How many different feelings do you think you will draw today? Will you feel the same thing all day? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many feelings you will draw today. One? Six? Why do you think so?

good: I am happy today, so I will be happy all day.
I get cross when I have to stop playing.

flow.parent: Many children guess one or two feelings, often 'happy all day'. Any guess is fine. Write it down, because you will compare it with the chart tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Do the first check now. 2. Your child stands still, puts one hand on their tummy and closes their eyes. 3. They name the feeling, then draw its face in circle 1.
flow.say: Stand still. Put your hand on your tummy. Close your eyes. What are you feeling right now? Is it small, middle or big?
flow.kid: Stand still. Hand on your tummy. Close your eyes. What do you feel? Is it small, middle or big? Draw its face.

ask.q: What are you feeling? How big is it?

flow.parent: Let your child choose the word. If they are stuck, offer three: 'Happy, sleepy or cross?' Do not tell them what they feel. Show 'how big' with your hands: close together, a bit apart, wide apart.

flow.do: 1. Stop at breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, late afternoon and bedtime. 2. Each time, your child names the feeling and draws the face. 3. Ask what was happening, and write one word next to the circle.
flow.say: Time to stop again. Hand on your tummy. What are you feeling now? What is happening just now?
flow.kid: Stop again. Hand on your tummy. What do you feel now? Draw it.
flow.wait: Do the other five checks through the day, about 2 minutes each
flow.parent: A phone alarm helps you remember. If you miss one time, do it as soon as you remember. Feelings in the middle of a cross moment are the most useful ones to draw.

flow.do: If your child draws a sad, cross or scared face, try one helper together. Then ask how the feeling is now. Draw the helper next to the circle.
flow.say: That is a cross face. Shall we try something that helps? Five slow breaths, a hug, or telling me what happened? How does the feeling feel now?
flow.kid: Is it a sad, cross or scared face? Try one helper. A slow breath, a hug, or telling someone. Is the feeling smaller now?
flow.parent: Do not hurry the feeling away. The point is to notice what happens to it. If no sad or cross face comes today, that is a real result too.

flow.do: Next day, look at the whole chart together. Count how many different faces there are. Read out the guess from yesterday.
flow.say: Look at your chart. How many different feelings did you draw? What was your guess? Did any feeling stay all day?
flow.kid: Look at your chart. Count the different faces. Did any feeling stay all day? Was your guess right?

ask.q: Did any feeling stay all day?
good: No. I was happy, then cross, then calm.
Happy came back two times, but other feelings came in between.

ask.q: What happened to the cross or sad face?
good: It went away after a hug.
The next face was a happy one.

flow.parent: Most children draw several different feelings in a day. If your child drew the same face six times, ask whether it was the same size each time, or try the chart again on a school day or a busy day.

flow.do: Ask your child to say it in three parts: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me like a scientist. What do you think about feelings now? What did your chart show? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say it like a scientist. What do you think now? What did your chart show? Why?

good: I think feelings change. My chart had four different faces. So no feeling stayed all day.
The cross feeling went away. After the slow breaths, the next face was calm.

flow.think: If feelings change all day, what can you do the next time a big angry feeling comes?

activities.title: Name It, Size It: how big is my feeling?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up tells short stories, and you name the feeling you would have. Then you show how big the feeling is with your hands.

materials.item: nothing but your hands and your voice

schedule.what: Name the feeling for six short stories, and show how big each one is.

activities.record: Draw your three biggest feelings from the game.

setup.art: A grown-up sitting on the floor facing a child, telling a story with open hands.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up tells a short story.

setup.art: A child holding both hands wide apart to show a big feeling, with a cross face.
setup.caption: 2. Name the feeling. Show how big it is with your hands.

flow.do: Show the three sizes with your hands: hands nearly touching for small, a little apart for middle, wide apart for big.
flow.say: Feelings have names, and they have sizes too. Small is like this. Middle is like this. Big is like this.
flow.kid: Feelings have names. They have sizes too. Small, middle, big. Show me with your hands.
flow.parent: Sizing a feeling helps a child notice that the same feeling can be small or big, and can change size.

flow.do: Tell these stories one at a time: your balloon bursts. Your friend says, 'I will not play with you.' You are told it is bedtime while you are still playing. Your teacher gives you a gold star. A cousin you love goes home after the holidays. The lights go out in a power cut.
flow.say: Listen to this. Your balloon bursts. What would you feel? How big is it? Show me.
flow.kid: Listen to the story. What would you feel? Say the name. Show how big.

ask.q: What would you feel? How big?

flow.parent: There is no wrong answer. One child feels sad about the burst balloon and another feels cross. Some stories bring two feelings at once, like sad and angry.

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: Can a big feeling become a small feeling? What could help it get smaller?
flow.kid: Can a big feeling get small? What could help?

activities.title: The Settling Bottle: watch it, and breathe
activities.context: In this activity you make a bottle of water with something in it that swirls and then settles. When a feeling is big, you shake it and watch it settle while you breathe slowly.

materials.item: a clean plastic bottle with a tight cap, about half a litre

materials.qty: to fill the bottle almost to the top

materials.item: something that sinks slowly: a spoon of rava, a spoon of used and cooled tea leaves, or glitter if you have it
a drop of food colour or a pinch of haldi, if you like

schedule.what: Make the bottle, shake it, and breathe slowly while it settles.

activities.record: Draw the bottle just after shaking, and again when it has settled.

setup.art: A child pouring a spoon of rava through a paper funnel into a plastic bottle of water, with a grown-up holding the bottle.
setup.caption: 1. Put water and a spoon of rava in the bottle. Close it tight.

setup.art: A child shaking the bottle hard, with the water inside all cloudy and swirling.
setup.caption: 2. Shake it hard. Everything swirls.

setup.art: A child sitting still, holding the bottle on their lap, breathing out slowly, with the rava settled at the bottom and the water clear.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it still. Breathe slowly until it settles.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle almost to the top with water. 2. Your child adds one spoon of rava or tea leaves, and the colour if you like. 3. Close the cap tightly.
flow.say: We are making a settling bottle. Pour in the rava. Now let's close it tight.
flow.kid: Pour the rava into the water. Close the cap tight.
flow.parent: Rava sinks in about 20 to 30 seconds. Used tea leaves, rinsed, take about the same. Glitter takes longer. Check the cap is tight so it does not leak.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes the bottle hard. 2. They hold it still and watch. 3. Breathe slowly together while you watch, in through the nose and out through the mouth.
flow.say: Shake it hard. Now hold it still. Watch the rava. Let's breathe slowly while it settles. In, and out.
flow.kid: Shake it hard. Now hold it still. Watch. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly.

ask.q: What happens when you keep it still?
good: The rava sinks to the bottom.

flow.parent: Count the breaths together. Most children take about four to six slow breaths before the rava has sunk. If it settles too fast, shake and breathe again.

flow.do: Talk about when to use it. Keep the bottle in a place your child can reach.
flow.say: When you feel very cross or upset, you can shake the bottle, watch it, and breathe. How do you feel after watching it settle?
flow.kid: When a feeling is big, shake the bottle. Watch it. Breathe slowly. How do you feel now?

ask.q: How do you feel after watching it?

flow.parent: The bottle does not change a feeling by itself. Watching it gives your child something to look at while they breathe slowly, and gives the feeling time to change. Some children like it; some prefer a hug. Both are fine.

activities.title: Tiger Body, Cat Body: feel your heart and breath change
activities.context: In this activity you stomp like an angry tiger, then rest like a sleepy cat. You feel your heart and your breath each time. A big feeling changes your body in the same kind of way.

materials.item: a little space to stomp in, and a mat or bed to lie on

schedule.what: Stomp, feel your heart, rest and breathe slowly, then feel it again.

activities.record: Draw yourself as a tiger and as a cat. Draw a big heart next to the tiger and a small, slow heart next to the cat.

setup.art: A child stomping on the spot with arms up like tiger claws, face scrunched up in a roar.
setup.caption: 1. Stomp like an angry tiger for 30 counts.

setup.art: A child sitting still with one hand flat on their chest, feeling their heart.
setup.caption: 2. Hand on your chest. Feel your heart.

setup.art: A child lying curled up on a mat like a cat, breathing slowly with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 3. Lie down like a sleepy cat. Breathe slowly. Feel again.

flow.do: Your child stomps on the spot and roars like an angry tiger while you count to 30.
flow.say: Be an angry tiger! Stomp and roar while I count to thirty.
flow.kid: Be an angry tiger. Stomp and roar. Keep going until thirty.
flow.parent: Neighbours below? Stomp softly on a mat, or do fast tiger claws and jumping jacks instead.

flow.do: Your child puts one hand flat on their chest. Ask what they feel.
flow.say: Stop. Put your hand flat on your chest. What is your heart doing? What is your breath doing?
flow.kid: Stop. Hand on your chest. What is your heart doing? Your breath?

good: My heart is going thump thump fast.

flow.do: Your child lies down like a sleepy cat. Breathe slowly together for one minute: in through the nose, out through the mouth.
flow.say: Now be a sleepy cat. Curl up. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Breathe out slowly through your mouth.
flow.kid: Be a sleepy cat. Curl up. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly.
flow.parent: One minute is about eight to ten slow breaths.

flow.do: Your child feels their chest again. Then explain the link to feelings.
flow.say: Feel your heart again. Is it faster or slower now? When you feel angry or scared, your heart beats fast like the tiger's, even sitting still. Slow breaths help your body calm down.
flow.kid: Feel your heart again. Is it slower? Angry feelings make your heart fast too. Slow breaths help it calm down.

check.q: You lay down like a cat and breathed slowly. What is your heart doing now?
check.why: Slow breaths let the body settle, so the heart beats slower than after the tiger. Fast stomping made it fast.

flow.parent: Be honest with your child: the tiger heart came from stomping, not from anger. But anger and fear also make the heart beat fast and the breath quick, and slow breathing helps the body settle.

activities.title: My Helping Hand: five things that help me
activities.context: In this activity you draw round your hand. On each finger you draw one thing that helps you when you feel sad or angry.

schedule.what: Draw round your hand and fill each finger with a helper.

activities.record: Your helping hand, stuck up where you can see it.

setup.art: A grown-up drawing round a child's spread hand on a sheet of paper with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round your hand.

setup.art: A paper hand with a small drawing on each finger: lungs breathing, two people hugging, a mouth talking, a tumbler of water, a quiet corner with a cushion.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one helper on each finger.

flow.do: Draw round your child's hand on the paper, with the fingers spread out.
flow.say: Spread your fingers on the paper. I will draw round your hand.
flow.kid: Spread your fingers. Keep your hand still while it is drawn.

flow.do: Your child draws one helper on each finger. Offer ideas only if they are stuck.
flow.say: When you feel sad or angry, what helps you? Draw one thing on each finger.
flow.kid: What helps when you feel sad or angry? Draw one thing on each finger.
flow.parent: Ideas, if needed: slow breaths, a hug, telling someone, a drink of water, a rest, a quiet corner, the settling bottle, crying. Leave out hitting or throwing things: tell your child gently that these hurt people and keep anger going.

flow.do: Stick the hand on the wall. Next time your child is upset, look at it together and pick one finger.
flow.say: Next time you feel sad or cross, we can look at your helping hand and pick a finger. Which one would you try first?
flow.kid: Next time you feel sad or cross, look at your hand. Pick a finger. Which one first?

games.title: What Would You Feel? A feelings card game
games.players: 2 or more players: a grown-up and a child, and anyone else who wants to play
games.context: This is a card game about naming feelings. Each card tells a short story. You say the feeling you would have, and show it with your face and body.

items.f: Your ice cream falls on the floor.
items.b: Many children feel sad or cross. Some laugh!

items.f: Your best friend comes to play.
items.b: Most children feel happy or excited.

items.f: A loud thunderclap wakes you up at night.
items.b: Many children feel scared. Some feel excited by storms.

items.f: Someone takes your crayons without asking.
items.b: Most children feel angry. That is fair: it was not kind.

items.f: A grown-up you love gives you a big hug.
items.b: Most children feel happy, warm or calm.

items.f: You lose a race at school.
items.b: Many children feel sad or cross. Some feel proud they tried.

items.f: You are going on a train to see your cousins tomorrow.
items.b: Most children feel excited. Some feel a bit nervous too.

items.f: Your kite string snaps and the kite floats away.
items.b: Many children feel sad. Some feel cross.

items.f: You learn to ride a cycle without help.
items.b: Most children feel proud and happy.

items.f: A big dog runs towards you, barking.
items.b: Many children feel scared. Children who love dogs may feel happy.

items.f: Another child tears your drawing.
items.b: Most children feel angry, and sad too. Two feelings can come at once.

items.f: It is your birthday, and everyone sings for you.
items.b: Most children feel happy. Some feel shy too.

items.f: A grown-up goes out, and you are not allowed to go with them.
items.b: Many children feel sad or cross.

items.f: You lie on the bed and listen to the rain.
items.b: Many children feel calm, or sleepy.

items.f: You can't find your favourite toy anywhere.
items.b: Many children feel worried, then cross.

items.f: Your friend shares her lunch when you forgot yours.
items.b: Most children feel happy and thankful.

printables.title: 6 feeling cards to cut out and draw

items.f: Happy
items.b: A smiling face with bright eyes.

items.f: Sad
items.b: A face with the mouth turned down and a tear.

items.f: Angry
items.b: A face with eyebrows pulled down and lips pressed tight.

items.f: Scared
items.b: A face with wide eyes and raised eyebrows.

items.f: Calm
items.b: A face with soft eyes and a small, quiet smile.

items.f: Excited
items.b: A face with a big open smile and eyebrows up.

rules: Cut out the six feeling cards. Draw the face on each one, using the hint on its back. Lay them in a row, face up. Mix the 16 story cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. The player whose turn it is gives the top story card to another player to read aloud. A child who cannot read yet gives it to the grown-up.
The player says what they would feel, and puts a finger on that feeling card.
The player shows the feeling with their face and body for three counts.
Everyone else says what they would feel. It is fine to feel something different.
The reader reads the back of the story card. Put the card face up in a used pile.

When all 16 story cards are used, each player picks one used card that gave a sad, cross or scared feeling, and says what would help. Then the game is over. Nobody wins or loses: you all named your feelings.

setup.art: Six face cards in a row on a floor mat, with a pile of story cards face down beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the six faces. Put the story cards in a pile.

setup.art: A child pointing at the angry face card and making an angry face, while a grown-up holds up a story card.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the story. Point to your feeling and show it.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Draw the face on each of the six feeling cards, using the hint on its back. Lay them in a row and read each name aloud together.
flow.say: These are six feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared, calm and excited. Let's draw each face and make it ourselves.
flow.kid: Here are six feelings. Say each name. Make each face.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules. Read each story card aloud.
flow.say: Listen: someone takes your crayons without asking. What would you feel? Point to the face. Now show it!
flow.kid: Listen to the story. What would you feel? Point to the face. Show it with your body.

good: No. I felt cross and the other player felt sad.
Some people like dogs and some are scared.

flow.parent: When two players feel differently, say so warmly: 'You felt scared and I felt excited. Both are real feelings.'

flow.do: At the end, each player chooses one card and says what would help.
flow.say: Pick one card that gave a sad or angry feeling. What would help you feel better?
flow.kid: Pick a sad or angry card. What would help you?

check.q: Another child tears your drawing. You feel angry. What helps most?
options: Telling them, 'I am angry. That was my drawing.'
check.why: Saying the feeling in words lets the other child know, and often makes the anger smaller. Tearing their drawing hurts them and keeps the anger going. Pretending hides the feeling but does not help it change.

games.title: Feeling Statues: freeze, then find a helper
games.players: 2 or more players: a grown-up calls the cards and a child dances. The grown-up can dance too.
games.context: This is a moving game. You dance while the music plays. When it stops, the grown-up calls a feeling, and you freeze like a statue showing that feeling with your whole body.

printables.title: 8 feeling call cards for the grown-up

items.f: Happy
items.b: Helper call: Share your happy with someone. Give them a high five.

items.f: Sad
items.b: Helper call: Give yourself a hug.

items.f: Angry
items.b: Helper call: Breathe out slowly, like blowing on hot rasam.

items.f: Scared
items.b: Helper call: Hold a grown-up's hand.

items.f: Calm
items.b: Helper call: Sit down and stay still for three counts.

items.f: Excited
items.b: Helper call: Jump three times, then stand still.

items.f: Tired
items.b: Helper call: Lie down and close your eyes for three counts.

items.f: Proud
items.b: Helper call: Stand tall and say, 'I did it!'

rules: Play music on a phone. Everyone dances.
The grown-up stops the music and calls the feeling on the top card.
Everyone freezes like a statue, showing that feeling with their face and whole body.
The grown-up reads the helper call on the back. Everyone does it.
Start the music again, and use the next card. After the eighth card, the game is over.

setup.art: Two children dancing in a living room while a woman holds a phone playing music.
setup.caption: 1. Dance while the music plays.

setup.art: Two children frozen as statues, one slumped and sad, one with fists up and an angry face.
setup.caption: 2. Music stops: freeze as the feeling. Then do the helper.

flow.do: Play by the rules. Use all eight cards.
flow.say: Dance! ... Stop! Freeze like a statue: ANGRY! Now the helper: breathe out slowly, like blowing on hot rasam.
flow.kid: Dance! When the music stops, freeze. Show the feeling with your whole body.
flow.parent: Notice how a body changes with each feeling: an angry statue is tight, a sad statue droops, a calm statue is soft.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which statue was hardest to do? Which helper made you feel calmest?
flow.kid: Which statue was hardest? Which helper made you calm?

good: Lying down with my eyes closed.

projects.title: One Week of Feelings and Helpers
projects.context: In this project, every evening for a week, you draw one big feeling from your day and what helped. At the end you look back at the whole week.

materials.item: a small notebook, or 7 sheets of paper stapled together

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw today's biggest feeling and what helped, or what made it.
Draw today's biggest feeling and what helped.
Draw today's biggest feeling and what helped.
Draw today's biggest feeling and what helped.
Draw today's biggest feeling and what helped.
Draw today's biggest feeling and what helped.
Draw the last page. Look at the whole week. Which helper did you use most? Which worked best?

projects.record: Seven pages, each with one feeling face and one helper drawing.

setup.art: A child at bedtime on a bed, drawing in a small notebook, with a reading lamp on.
setup.caption: 1. Each evening, draw today's biggest feeling.

setup.art: An open notebook page with a sad face on the left and a drawing of two people hugging on the right.
setup.caption: 2. Next to it, draw what helped.

flow.do: Make the book. On page 1, your child draws today's biggest feeling and what helped, or what made it.
flow.say: What was the biggest feeling you had today? Draw its face. Did anything help? Draw that next to it.
flow.kid: What was your biggest feeling today? Draw the face. What helped? Draw that too.
flow.parent: Happy days count too: draw what made the happy feeling. On a hard day, keep it short and gentle.

flow.do: Each evening for the next five days, do one page.
flow.say: Time for your feelings book. What was your biggest feeling today? What helped?
flow.kid: Feelings book time. Biggest feeling today? What helped?
flow.wait: Do one page each evening, about 3 minutes

flow.do: On day 7, draw the last page. Then lay all the pages out and look at them together.
flow.say: Look at your whole week. Which feeling came most? Which helper did you use most? Which one worked best for you?
flow.kid: Look at your week. Which feeling came most? Which helper worked best?

good: Hugs, because they make me warm.
Telling a grown-up, because then they know.

flow.parent: There is no right helper. Different helpers work for different children, and for different feelings.

challenges.title: A Cheer-Up Box for Someone at Home
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Someone at home will feel sad one day. Can you make a box of things that might help them feel better?
challenges.problem: Make a small cheer-up box for someone in your family. Put in things that might help them when they feel sad or cross.
constraints: It must fit in a shoebox or a small carton.
Put in at least one thing to look at, one to touch and one to do.
materials: small things from home, like a soft toy, a photo, a smooth stone or a shell
general: A drawing or a note that says 'I love you'.
A family photo to look at.
A soft toy or a soft cloth to hold.
The settling bottle to shake and watch.
creative: A card with five slow breaths drawn on it, as five candles to blow out.
A recording on the phone of you singing their favourite song.
A 'joke jar' with three of your best jokes, drawn or told to a grown-up to write.
A coupon that says 'One free hug from me'.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose who your box is for. What helps them when they are sad? Make the box, and give it to them.

setup.art: A child decorating a shoebox with crayon drawings of hearts and suns.
setup.caption: 1. Decorate a box.

setup.art: An open shoebox with a soft toy, a family photo, a drawn card of five candles and a paper coupon saying 'One free hug'.
setup.caption: 2. Fill it with things that help.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask who the box is for and what helps them.
flow.say: Who at home would you like to make a cheer-up box for? When they feel sad, what helps them?
flow.kid: Who is your box for? What helps them when they are sad?

good: A younger brother likes his soft elephant.
My mother likes it when I hug her.

flow.do: Your child decorates the box. Then they fill it: one thing to look at, one to touch and one to do.
flow.say: Now put in one thing to look at, one thing to touch and one thing to do. Why will each one help?
flow.kid: Put in one thing to look at. One to touch. One to do. Why will each one help?
flow.parent: Help your child think about the other person: what helps your child might be different from what helps a grandparent.

flow.do: Your child gives the box and tells the person what it is for.
flow.say: Give your box, and tell them what it is for.
flow.kid: Give your box. Tell them what it is for.
flow.think: When that person feels sad, which thing in the box do you think they will pick first?

items.p: Draw a line from each face to its feeling name.
pairs: A face with a big smile
A face with eyebrows pulled down and lips tight
items.why: A smile often shows happy, a tear often shows sad, pulled-down eyebrows often show angry, and wide eyes often show scared. Faces give clues, but asking is the surest way to know.
items.art: Four faces on the left, four feeling words on the right.

items.p: Draw your face when you feel happy. Then draw your face when you feel cross.
items.a: Two faces: one smiling, one with eyebrows down or a frown.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two clearly different faces. The eyebrows and mouth change most.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side.

items.p: If you drew a face for how you feel six times in one day, what would the faces probably show?
opts: Many different feelings in one day
items.why: Feelings change through the day. A chart usually shows several different feelings.
items.context: This question is about a feelings chart. You stop six times in one day and draw a face for how you feel each time.

items.p: It is all right to feel angry sometimes.
items.why: True. Everyone feels angry sometimes. The feeling is all right. What matters is what we do with it.

items.p: Colour the things that help with anger green. Colour the things that make anger bigger red.
items: a drink of water and a rest
items.why: Slow breaths, talking and resting calm the body. Hitting, shouting and throwing keep the body hot and fast, and keep the anger going.
items.art: Six small pictures: a child breathing slowly, a child hitting, two children talking, a child shouting, a tumbler of water, a toy flying through the air.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: tell about a time you felt sad. What helped?
items.a: For example: 'I was sad when my fish died. A grown-up hugged me and we talked about him.'
items.why: A strong answer names the feeling, says what caused it, and names something that helped.

items.p: Anu, a girl of 6 in Hyderabad, is very angry because her cousin broke her toy.

views.says: Hit your pillow hard. That will get the anger out.
Sit with me and take five slow breaths. Then tell me what happened.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example: 'Anu's mother, because slow breaths calm your body, and scientists found that hitting things keeps anger going.' Then it is fair to the other side: Riya is right that hitting a pillow is better than hitting a person.
items.why: Scientists tested hitting things when angry, and found it usually keeps anger going. Calming the body and talking help more. But Riya's idea is kinder than hitting someone.

items.p: A feeling can be small, middle or big.
items.why: True. The same feeling can be small, middle or big, and it can change size.
items.context: This question is about sizing a feeling with your hands in Name It, Size It.

items.p: Here is a child who feels scared. Draw an arrow to where you might feel fear in your body, and say what it does.
items.a: Arrows to the heart (beats fast), the tummy (feels fluttery or tight), the eyes (open wide) or the legs (want to run).
items.why: Fear happens in the whole body. The heart beats faster and the body gets ready to run.
items.art: An outline of a child standing, with space around for arrows.

items.p: After Tiger Body, Cat Body, you stomped and then felt your chest. What was your heart doing?
items.why: Stomping made your heart beat fast. Anger and fear make the heart beat fast too. Slow breaths helped it slow down.
items.context: This question is about Tiger Body, Cat Body. You stomped like a tiger, then put a hand on your chest.

items.p: A girl builds a sandcastle. A wave knocks it down. She takes slow breaths and gets a hug. Then she builds it again. Put her feelings in order.
items.why: She is happy building her castle. She feels angry when it breaks. After slow breaths and a hug she feels calmer. She is happy again when she rebuilds it.
items.context: This question is about how feelings change as things happen.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: why does saying 'I am angry' help more than hitting?
items.a: Saying it lets people know how I feel, and it makes the anger smaller. Hitting hurts someone and keeps me angry.
items.why: A strong answer says that naming a feeling often makes it smaller and lets others help, and that hitting hurts people and keeps anger going.

items.p: Ravi, a boy of 7 in Pune, fell and hurt his knee in the park. He is crying.

views.says: Big boys don't cry. Stop crying.
It is all right to cry. It hurts. Come here and I will hold you.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person might be trying to do.
items.a: A strong answer picks Meera or the uncle with a reason. For example: 'Meera, because boys feel pain and sadness just like girls, and crying asks for comfort.' Then fair to the other side: the uncle may want Ravi to feel brave.
items.why: Boys and girls have the same feelings. Crying is a normal way to show hurt and to ask for comfort. The uncle may mean well, but hiding a feeling does not make it go away.

items.p: Draw a helper that would work for you when you feel scared at night.
items.a: For example: a night light, a hug, a soft toy, slow breaths.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one clear thing that helps, and the child can say why it helps.

items.p: Good children are happy all the time.
items.why: False. Every child feels sad, cross and scared sometimes. These feelings are normal, for good children too.

items.p: You see a friend sitting alone, looking sad. What could you say?
opts: Do you want to sit with me?
items.why: Asking kindly and sitting with someone comforts them. It shows you noticed their feeling.

items.p: Chinnu built five towers on her sandcastle. Then two towers fell down. How many towers were still standing?
items.why: 5 towers take away 2 that fell leaves 3.
items.context: This question is about Chinnu's Sandcastle, the story in this unit. Her boy broke two of her five towers.

items.p: Match each feeling with a helper that might work.
items.a: pairs as given, though other matches can be fair
items.why: A hug comforts sadness, slow breaths calm anger, holding a hand helps with fear, and rest helps tiredness. Many helpers work for more than one feeling.

items.p: Here is your Settling Bottle just after shaking, and a little later when it has settled. Say which is 'shaken' and which is 'settled', and a grown-up writes the words.
items.a: 'Shaken' under the cloudy bottle, 'settled' under the clearer one with rava at the bottom.
items.why: When shaken, the rava swirls and clouds the water. Kept still, it sinks and the water clears. Watching it gives a feeling time to change.
items.art: Two bottles: one cloudy and swirling, one clear with a layer of rava at the bottom.
items.context: This question is about the settling bottle, where you shook a bottle with rava in it and watched it settle.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: a dog wags her tail and jumps when her friend comes home. What feeling do you think the dog has? How can you tell?
items.a: Happy or excited, because the dog's whole body moves and the tail wags, just like I jump when I am happy.
items.why: A strong answer names a feeling and gives the evidence: what the dog does with their body. Scientists judge other animals' feelings the same way, by watching what they do.

quiz.p: Which of these is a feeling?
quiz.why: Scared is a feeling. A spoon is a thing, and blue is a colour.

quiz.p: Your heart beats fast and you want to run. Which feeling is this most likely to be?
quiz.why: Fear makes the heart beat fast and gets the body ready to run. Calm and sleepy make the body slow.

quiz.p: Is it all right to feel sad?
quiz.why: Everyone feels sad sometimes: children and grown-ups, girls and boys. It is a normal feeling.

quiz.p: Chinnu felt happy, then angry, then calm, then happy again, all on one afternoon at the beach. What does this show?
quiz.why: Chinnu's feelings changed again and again. Feelings come and go.

quiz.p: Selvi, a girl of 6, feels very angry. Which of these helps her calm down?
quiz.why: Slow breaths calm the body. Hitting hurts someone, and shouting keeps the anger going.

opts: In the whole body: heart, tummy, face and thoughts
quiz.why: A scared heart beats fast, an angry face gets hot, and a sad throat gets tight. Feelings happen in the whole body.

quiz.p: Your friend is crying because her balloon burst. What could you do to comfort her?
opts: Sit with her and ask if she wants a hug
quiz.why: Sitting with someone and offering a hug comforts them. Laughing or walking away can make them feel worse.

quiz.p: Why does saying 'I am cross' help?
opts: It often makes the feeling a little smaller, and others know how you feel
quiz.why: Scientists have found that putting a feeling into words often makes it a little smaller. It also lets others know, so they can help.

quiz.p: Chinnu's sandcastle was broken. She felt angry and sad at the same time. Can two feelings come at once?
opts: Yes, two feelings can come together
No, only one feeling at a time
quiz.why: Two or more feelings often come together, like angry and sad when something you made is broken.

quiz.p: A dog jumps and wags her tail when her friend comes home. What feeling does the dog most likely have?
quiz.why: A wagging tail and jumping usually show a happy, excited dog. Humans and other animals have feelings.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl of 6, made a feelings chart. It had 6 circles. She drew a happy face in 2 of them. How many circles had other feelings?
maths.explain: 6 circles take away the 2 happy ones leaves 4. So happy was only part of her day.
maths.context: This is about the feelings chart, where you drew a face six times in one day.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the happy faces shows how much of the day had other feelings.

maths.problem: Arjun, a boy of 6, drew these faces on his chart: happy, cross, happy, calm, sleepy, happy. Make a tally mark for each feeling. Which feeling came most often?
maths.answer: Happy came most often, 3 times. Cross, calm and sleepy came 1 time each.
maths.explain: Happy: 3 marks. Cross: 1. Calm: 1. Sleepy: 1. 3 is the biggest number, so happy came most.
maths.context: This is about a feelings chart like the one you made.
maths.why_maths: A tally lets you see at a glance which feeling came most in a day.

maths.problem: In the settling bottle, Fathima, a girl of 6, counted 6 slow breaths before the rava sank. Her friend Zoya counted 4. Who took more breaths? How many more?
maths.explain: 6 is more than 4. Count on from 4 to 6: 5, 6. That is 2 more. Slower breaths mean fewer breaths in the same time, so Zoya may have breathed more slowly.
maths.context: This is about the settling bottle, where you breathe slowly while the rava sinks.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts makes you think about why the numbers are different, when the bottle took the same time.

maths.problem: Look at your own chart. Which feeling did you draw first in the morning? Which did you draw last at bedtime? Were they the same?
maths.answer: Your own answer, for example: sleepy first, sleepy last, but different feelings in between.
maths.explain: Putting the faces in time order shows how a feeling changed from morning to night.
maths.context: This is about your own feelings chart.
maths.why_maths: Ordering the faces by time of day shows the feelings changing through the day.

videos.title: A short song about feelings: all our feelings are okay
videos.why: Shows faces and bodies for each feeling, and helps children learn the names.
videos.check: Found by search: "All Our Feelings Are Okay | Scribbles Crew Feelings Song for Kids | Emotional Literacy for Children" by The Scribbles Crew & Friends, 1 minute, 50 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Belly breathing for children
videos.why: Goes with Tiger Body, Cat Body and the settling bottle: a calm guide to breathing in and out slowly.
videos.check: Found by search: "Belly Breathing: Mindfulness for Children" by The Mindfulness Teacher, 4 minutes, 6 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Tickling a rat: scientists find out that rats laugh
videos.why: Shows that other animals have happy feelings too, and how scientists found out.
videos.check: Found by search: "See What Happens When You Tickle a Rat" by National Geographic, 3 minutes, 19 seconds. A parent may preview it.

applications: Many schools in India now hold short feelings or happiness classes. Delhi government schools began a Happiness Curriculum in 2018.
Doctors and counsellors teach slow breathing to children and grown-ups who feel very worried or angry.
Teachers in many classrooms keep a calm corner where a child can go to sit quietly when a feeling is big.
Parents and teachers ask 'What are you feeling?' to help small children name a feeling before it turns into a tantrum.

spotted.art: A row of people in a cinema hall, some laughing, one crying, one with hands over their mouth.

spotted.text: A pet dog jumping and wagging her tail at the door when a family member comes home.
spotted.art: A dog jumping at the front door of a flat as a woman comes in with shopping bags.

spotted.text: A touch-me-not plant on a roadside or in a pot, folding up their leaves when touched.
spotted.art: A child's finger touching a touch-me-not plant, with the leaves folding up.

open_questions.q: Exactly why does naming a feeling make it smaller?
open_questions.why_open: Brain scans show that naming a feeling quietens a part of the brain linked to fear. Scientists are still finding out how this happens, and why it works more for some people than others.

open_questions.q: How many different feelings are there?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think there are a few basic feelings that everyone has. Others think every language and every person puts feelings together in their own way. Nobody agrees yet.

open_questions.q: What do other beings feel, from crows and ants to plants?
open_questions.why_open: We can watch what they do and measure changes in their bodies, but we cannot be inside them. Scientists argue about how like ours their feelings are.

warmup.q: Is it all right to feel angry?
warmup.a: Yes. Everyone feels angry sometimes. What we do with it matters.

warmup.q: Your heart beats fast and your eyes open wide. What feeling might it be?
Name one thing that helps when you feel sad.
warmup.a: A hug, telling someone, a rest, crying, slow breaths.

warmup.q: Does a feeling stay all day?
warmup.a: No. Feelings change many times in a day.

science: B. J. Bushman, 'Does venting anger feed or extinguish the flame? Catharsis, rumination, distraction, anger, and aggressive responding', Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 28(6), 724-731, 2002. About 600 students; rumination group angriest and most aggressive; control group (no punching bag) least.

S. L. Kjærvik and B. J. Bushman, 'A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage?', Clinical Psychology Review, 2024. 154 studies, about 10,000 participants; arousal-decreasing activities reduced anger.

M. D. Lieberman, N. I. Eisenberger, M. J. Crockett, S. M. Tom, J. H. Pfeifer and B. M. Way, 'Putting feelings into words: affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli', Psychological Science 18(5), 421-428, 2007.

L. F. Barrett and colleagues on emotional granularity: people who describe feelings with finer words regulate negative feelings better (for example Barrett, Gross, Christensen and Benvenuto, Cognition and Emotion, 2001).
J. Panksepp and J. Burgdorf: young rats make 50 kHz chirps when tickled, which they described as a form of laughter (studies from the late 1990s and 2000s).
Consolation after fights in chimpanzees: F. de Waal and A. van Roosmalen, 1979.

roots.context: We have named our feelings and drawn them six times in one day. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves, and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: On your chart you drew several different faces in one day. A cross or sad face did not stay. Each time, the same child stopped and noticed the feeling. So a feeling comes and goes, and the child who has it stays.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'I am angry' or 'she is a sad child', as if a feeling were a fixed part of a person. The chart shows a feeling is something that happens to you for a while, and then changes.
deep_truth.evidence: Count the different faces on your own chart, and look at which face came after each cross or sad face.

three.who_am_i: You are the one who feels happy, cross, sleepy and calm. The feelings change, and you are still you.
three.what_is_life: Living beings feel. A child, a dog and a rat being tickled all feel and respond to what happens to them. A touch-me-not plant responds to touch too.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of feeling beings, each having feelings that come and go, just as yours do.

roots.thread: In one day you felt sleepy, happy, cross and calm. The same child noticed each feeling. Feelings come and go, and the one who notices them stays. Other living beings have feelings that come and go too.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, joy and sorrow, come from the senses meeting the world. They come and they go, and they do not last. So bear them patiently.
teachings.link: Your feelings chart showed the same thing: joy and sorrow came and went in one day. Waiting patiently with a feeling lets it change.

teachings.teaching: Hatred is never ended by more hatred. It is ended only by letting go of hatred.
teachings.link: Scientists found the same about anger: hitting and shouting keep anger going. Calming down lets it go.

teachings.teaching: Let go of anger towards anyone, because harmful things come from it.
teachings.link: Anger is a normal feeling. But when we act on it by hitting or shouting, we and other people get hurt. Letting it settle first helps everyone.

science.text: Calming the body, with slow breathing or relaxing, makes anger smaller. Hitting things while angry usually keeps anger going. More than 150 studies show this.
Naming a feeling often makes it a little smaller. Exactly why is still being studied.

other_view.view: Waiting for a feeling to pass is not always enough. A sad or angry feeling often means something really is wrong, like unfair treatment or a lost friend. Then the problem needs fixing, or the feeling keeps coming back.

practice.title: Watch a feeling change
practice.say: Sit still with me. Close your eyes. Put your hand on your tummy. What feeling is here right now? Say its name quietly. Now breathe in slowly, and out slowly, five times. Let's count together. Now look again. Is the feeling the same, or has it changed a little? You noticed a feeling come and change. You were here all the time.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Hand on your tummy. What feeling is here? Say its name. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Do it five times. Is the feeling the same now? Or has it changed?

ask: When your feeling changed from cross to calm, where did the cross feeling go?
Are you your feelings, or the one who has them?
If a crow and a dog have feelings too, what might make them happy?

playtest: Walked through every activity, the feelings chart, both games, the project and the challenge as a parent and a six-year-old in a flat; they need only paper, crayons, a plastic bottle and a spoon of rava, and the step minutes add up. Games work with 2 and with 4 players and every card is written out. Fixed a quiz answer that marked the wrong option, a sorting question that gave away its own order, a count question that used breaths the story never mentions, an ice-cream note for a story that has none, a repeated cousin story and a repeated hitting question, and removed assumed brothers.
